extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and classics; general educated readers interested in Plato
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative criteria and practical guidance from a critical account of Plato's educational, medical, legal, and political doctrines (mainly Republic, Laws, and related dialogues). Useful for assessing Platonic theory or construing principles for education, law, and medicine derived from Plato.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the use of fiction in early education
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘We should limit the use of fiction by the necessity of the case.’ The child must be taught some things in figure only, but fiction should be used sparingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach simple religious and moral truths first as principles; avoid inculcating stories (e.g., the lusts and treacheries of the gods) that may corrupt youth or set bad behavioural models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach truth as principle rather than mere fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato’s aim: early education is ‘not truth as a matter of fact, but truth as a matter of principle’—instill general moral and religious principles before particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize enduring moral concepts and good manners/taste over factual detail at the earliest stages; use simplified, principle-focused instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect upbringing from harmful sights and sounds
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The young are to be brought up in happy surroundings, out of the way of sights or sounds which may hurt the character or vitiate the taste.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an atmosphere of health (physical and moral); avoid exposing children to corrosive cultural influences that undermine character formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as harmonious growth; simplicity as first principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should aim for ‘harmonious growth, in which are insensibly learnt the lessons of temperance and endurance, and the body and mind develope in equal proportions.’ Simplicity runs through all art and life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure curricula to balance bodily and intellectual development; favor simple forms and rules in art, training, and legislation to cultivate temperance and endurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate periods for physical (gymnastic) and literary training
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato separates ‘the time of training’ for gymnastic entirely from literary education, believing two opposite natures cannot be learned at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simultaneous intensive physical and intellectual training in the same period; be cautious of overtraining the body at the expense of the intellect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use music and gymnastic to improve the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrary to common opinion, music and gymnastic are ‘both equally designed for the improvement of the mind’; the body is ‘the servant of the mind.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat physical and musical education as means to cultivate mental qualities (discipline, continuity of exertion), not merely bodily fitness or entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simplicity in medical practice; treat whole person
rubrics_metrics.description: Medicine has a demand ‘for greater simplicity’; Plato holds that ‘the eye cannot be cured without the rest of the body, nor the body without the mind.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize basic conditions of health (air, water, baths) and preventive care; beware of treatments that complicate or enlarge diseases by over-intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physician qualifications should include personal experience of disease
rubrics_metrics.description: The physician ‘should have, in modern phraseology, a nervous temperament; he should have experience of disease in his own person, in order that his powers of observation may be quickened.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value clinical empathy and firsthand experience as elements that sharpen diagnostic observation and practical wisdom in physicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawmaking should follow the golden rule of simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: In law, Plato advocates simplicity: ‘Greater matters are to be determined by the legislator or by the oracle of Delphi, lesser matters are to be left to the temporary regulation of the citizens themselves.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrate authoritative lawmaking on major, fundamental issues; allow local/custom regulation for minor matters; avoid over-legislation that complicates governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention over extirpation in public remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The diseases of a State are like the heads of a hydra; they multiply when they are cut off. The true remedy for them is not extirpation but prevention.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address root causes (education, social conditions) rather than punitive or piecemeal removal of symptoms; favor preventive public policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: National education as the primary political measure
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The only political measure worth having—the only one which would produce any certain or lasting effect, was a measure of national education.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize broad educational reform as foundational to political and social improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate the habit of abstraction via mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The great aim of education is the cultivation of the habit of abstraction. This is to be acquired through the study of the mathematical sciences.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mathematics to train the mind in relation, proportion, and abstract thinking; value its role in organizing particulars into general principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectic as the highest science toward the Idea of Good
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialectic is ‘the science which... divides a whole into the natural parts, and reunites the scattered parts into a natural or organized whole... which pierces the veil of hypotheses and reaches the final cause or first principle of all.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote dialectical enquiry (Socratic interrogative) as the advanced method for grasping universal essences and unity; see dialogues as models of this method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits and possible vacuity of metaphysical ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: The Idea of Good is ‘a mere vision of which no distinct explanation can be given’ and an ‘abstraction under which no individuals are comprehended.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat grand metaphysical ideals as guiding visions that may lack concrete content; use them to inspire direction but not as finished scientific explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for individual differences in education
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism: Plato ‘does not see that education is relative to the characters of individuals; he only desires to impress the same form of the state on the minds of all.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid one-size-fits-all curricula; allow freedom and ‘a little wholesome neglect’ to permit individual development and character formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote lifelong self-education with modest, steady gains
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-education consists in many ‘commonplace’ acts: choose a branch that suits the mind, study great authors, add to nature by slow additions, and ‘creep on quietly from one thing to another.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage daily, manageable study (e.g., an hour a day), select topics aligned with vocation or contrast to it, beware of vanity or chasing illusory grand schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of doctrinaire uniformity and intolerance of innovators
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato’s intolerance: desire that citizens ‘remain within the lines which he has laid down’ and zeal against innovators in religion or politics; reservations about changing fundamental institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the value of institutional stability against the need for reform; be cautious about suppressing innovation wholesale while preserving core virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Plato’s works by comparative literary and doctrinal criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between Republic and Laws: Republic = hope, dramatic power, intellectual; Laws = failure/old age, sermonic, more religious, less presence of doctrines (e.g., doctrine of ideas absent, immortality first mentioned later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing Platonic dialogues, consider tone (aspirational vs. resigned), rhetorical/dramatic quality, presence of core doctrines, treatment of poets, and practical detail vs. idealism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize ancient views on progress and institutional change
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancients (including Plato) lacked a modern idea of steady progress; they treated laws as inviolate and were ‘puzzled by Egyptian monuments,’ leading to conservative attitudes toward change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret Platonic conservatism in light of limited historical perspective; do not anachronistically expect modern notions of historical progress when evaluating ancient political thought.
